title: Sweep Picking
goal: Sweep clean, separated arpeggios from three-string triads to six-string shapes, and link them through minor-key progressions so they sound like a solo.
assumes: You can alternate-pick single notes evenly at sixteenths around 80 BPM (Alternate Picking through its Intermediate Level covers this) and you can hammer on and pull off cleanly. It helps to know what a triad is and which note makes it major or minor (Triads through its Intermediate Level covers this, and Step 1 here says it briefly). You don't need any sweeping yet, and you can start at whichever Level suits you.

skills: Even alternate picking at sixteenths, 80 BPM

orderRationale: Three Levels, each open from the start, rebuilt on 2026-11-17 after the owner played the old Step 1 (two notes, mostly rests, at 50 BPM) and called it a beginner exercise nobody should have to sit through. Beginner now starts on a real sweep: a three-string A minor triad up and down in triplets, with one beat of rest only where it teaches the muting reset. It is the standard first drill in most sweep courses (one push per click, the top note repeated where the pick turns), and it already sounds like an arpeggio. A minor and C major come together in the first Step because their shapes differ by one note, and the Step says they are two different chords; C major against C minor, the pair that does differ by its third, is one of its Takes. Then the turn at the top with a hammer and a pull, which is what removes the repeated note; then phrases, then the three inversions; and the Level ends with a four-bar solo over a band. Intermediate skips everything under four strings: four-string shapes, then the five-string A-shape, then the E-shape with a hammer or a tap at the top, then inversions and position shifts with those shapes, and only then linking, which the owner asked for as the backbone, on three strings first because a long shape makes a bad link worse: the link, chains of links, then the minor-key progressions with the major five chord, and only after those the four- and five-string chains. It ends on an eight-bar etude over a band. Advanced adds six strings, first shape by shape and then as whole shapes through chord changes, wide shifts and neoclassical sequences, and a composed eight-bar etude before the heavy band. The comparison was against common practice (Gambale's economy and sweep method, Becker- and Malmsteen-style arpeggio studies, Troy Grady's work on pick paths): triads before long shapes, the turnaround as its own skill, the tap as an extension of the five-string shape. Chains change chord once a bar because Jam's grid is one chord to a bar. The progressions are common vocabulary and every line is written for this Path: nothing is transcribed from a song or copied from a course.
gradingLimits: Grading stops being trustworthy at about 150 ms between notes: sixteenths at 100 BPM, eighth triplets at 133, sextuplets at 66. Rungs faster than that are self-checked, whatever they look like, and the card says where grading stops. That line is a cautious policy, not a measurement. What a sweep is graded on is timing: how even the notes are, whether each one arrived, and whether extra notes crept in. Right notes are not graded anywhere on this Path: swept notes ring into each other, and a pitch read on ringing strings can fail a take that was played right, so nothing here promises them. The tests behind these numbers used synthetic tones, and no real guitar has been through them yet. The note after a slide counts as missed if it isn't heard, so bars on sliding shapes are lower; a tap counts as a note that must be heard, and a hammer or pull that isn't heard costs nothing. In practice: Beginner is graded at nearly every rung, and its one sextuplet phrase is self-checked. In Intermediate the sixteenth-note shapes stop at 100 BPM and triplet shapes at 130. In Advanced most of what makes the playing hard can't be graded. Sound never tells us the two things that matter most here, muting and pick path, and the Exercises say so.

steps.title: Three-string triads, up and down
steps.goal: Sweep a minor and a major triad on the top three strings, up and back down, in even triplets, with each note separate.
steps.why: This is the sweep everyone recognises: three notes of a chord in one push, A, C, E going up and E, C, A coming back. Three strings is the size every bigger shape is made of, and it's short enough to keep clean from the first day. Triplets put one sweep on every click, so the rhythm tells you where each stroke starts. You learn a minor and a major triad together because their shapes differ by one note, and hearing that note is what turns a shape into a chord you can use.
howTo: One push per click. Going up the strings, the pick falls through the G, B and E strings in one downward motion and comes to rest on each string before it plays it. Coming back, the same in reverse: one upward pull through E, B and G. The last Exercise turns the pick at both ends with no repeated note, in sixteenths.
The top note is played twice, once at the end of the push and once at the start of the pull. That repeated note is the only place the pick changes direction.

Fretting hand: lift each finger's pressure as soon as the next note sounds, without leaving the string. Picking hand: the side of the palm rests lightly on the strings you have just left. Those two together are the mute.

A triad is a chord of three notes: the root, which is the note the chord is named after, the third and the fifth. A minor is A (the root), C (the third) and E (the fifth). Its shape at fret 12: ring finger on the G string at 14, middle finger on the B string at 13, index on the top string at 12. Move the G string note to fret 12 and the notes are G, C and E. That is C major, a different chord that shares two notes with A minor.

The third is the note that makes a triad major or minor. C major is C, E and G. Lower the E by one fret and it is C minor: that pair is one of the Takes of the second Exercise. If this is new, the Triads Path teaches it slowly, through its Intermediate Level.
steps.payoff: A minor and C major arpeggios that sound like chords being spelled out, and a four-chord progression played as sweeps, in your first session.

howTo: Triplets: two notes, then a silent third. Push down through both strings in one motion; the pick lands on the second string, rests there for a moment, then goes through it. Coming back, one pull up through both.
On the B and top strings in A minor: middle finger on the B string at 13, index on the top string at 12. Let go of the first note as the second sounds, without lifting the finger off the string.

steps.title: The turn at the top: hammer and pull-off
steps.goal: Turn the sweep round at the top with a hammer and a pull, so it loops with no repeated note and no extra pick stroke.
steps.why: In the last Step the pick turned round on a repeated note, or by itself. Real sweep lines don't repeat the top note: they add one more chord tone on the top string with a hammer, pull back off it, and sweep down. The hammer and the pull give the pick a moment with nothing to do, which is exactly when it changes direction, so the turn can't be heard. This loop is the sound of a sweep in a solo, and three strings is the cheapest place to learn it.
howTo: After the top string's push, the next note is a hammer-on, so the pick has nothing to do. Use that moment to turn it round.
The pull-off back is the last note before the upward push begins. Keep the pull clean: pull slightly sideways, off the string, and do not just lift.
Start with C major: its reach on the top string is three frets. The minor shapes reach five, and they come next.
steps.payoff: A triad that loops without a seam, with the turn inaudible, at a tempo you can sing along with.

steps.title: Sweeps inside phrases
steps.goal: Use a sweep as part of a line that goes somewhere, starting and ending in a scale or on a held note.
steps.why: Nobody wants to hear ten bars of arpeggio. What makes a sweep sound exciting is what comes either side of it: a line that arrives by sweep, then sings; a run that shoots up to a held bend. This Step turns the shapes into something you could actually play in a solo.
howTo: Vibrato is a bend kept very small: push the string a little and let it back, over and over, at an even speed.
The held note after a sweep matters more than the sweep. Give it time and a little vibrato.
Change technique cleanly. When a sweep ends, you go straight back to normal picking, with no moment of confusion in the hand.
Use these as starting points. Write your own ending as soon as you can play the written one.
Blues and Pentatonics teaches the bend in its Step 'Bends that land'.
steps.payoff: Four phrases you can actually use in a solo, each one ending in a note that sings.

steps.title: Triads up the neck
steps.goal: Play the same minor and major triad in three places up the neck, with the shifts landing on time.
steps.why: A shape you know in one place is a shape you can only use in one place. Every triad has three shapes on the top three strings, one for each of its three notes at the bottom, called inversions, and between them they cover the neck, so whatever chord comes next, one of its shapes is under your hand. Learning them as loops that climb and come back is also your first real position-shift drill.
howTo: Name the notes out loud as you practise, at least once. The spelled notes on each Exercise are there for that.
Moving between inversions, shift during the last note of the bar, and arrive on the first finger of the new shape.
steps.payoff: A minor, C major and D minor in three places each, so the next chord always has a shape near your hand.

steps.title: Your first sweep solo, with the band
steps.goal: Play looped three-string triads through two progressions over a band, and a four-bar sweep solo that ends on a held note.
steps.why: Everything so far has been against a click. A band changes how it feels: the bass plays the roots, the drums carry the beat, and your arpeggios suddenly sound like a guitar solo instead of an exercise. howTo: Use direct input or headphones for a graded take. A microphone also hears the band, and that hasn't been tested.

steps.payoff: You play a sweep solo over a band that follows the chords and ends on a note that sings.

steps.title: Four strings
steps.goal: Add the D string without losing the separation you built on three.
steps.why: Four strings is enough for a full-sounding chord and short enough to keep clean. A longer push means more time for an earlier note to keep ringing, so it is the first real test of your muting. It's also the first place the pick travels far enough that the arm has to carry it, not the wrist.
howTo: Let the forearm carry the pick across. The wrist stays still.
The palm mute now has to travel with the pick, and the fretting hand keeps releasing each note in turn.
The bottom note is played once: you arrive on it with the upward push and leave it with a downstroke on the next string. Keep that change small.
steps.payoff: A sweep that sounds like a real chord being spelled out, at a tempo you can sing, in four shapes.

steps.title: Five strings: the root positions
steps.goal: Own the two common five-string shapes with the root on the A string, in minor and major.
steps.why: Five strings is the big sweep, the sound people mean when they say the word. This Step has the shapes with the root on the A string, called the A-shape from here on: one minor and one major. Moved to another fret, those two give you every minor and major chord. The third Exercise adds one more major shape, and the next Step adds a second family.
howTo: Minor: root on the A string, a hammer to the third on that same string, then one note a string up to the top. Major: a chord tone below the root, a slide up to the root, then one note a string.
Mute everything. With five strings moving there is more to keep silent than there are fingers: palm on the low strings, fretting fingers across the high ones.
Keep this below your speed limit. A clean five-string sweep at a modest tempo sounds better than a fast smear.
steps.payoff: The sound you came for: a five-string arpeggio up the neck and back, with every note separate.

steps.title: Five strings: the E-shape, and a tap at the top
steps.goal: Sweep the E-shape arpeggios that start on the fifth, and add a tapped note above the top of a five-string shape.
steps.why: The A-shape puts the root on the A string. The E-shape is the barre chord with its root on the low E string, swept from the A string up, so it starts on the chord's fifth. The first two Exercises give the fingering. Between the two shapes you have a minor and a major arpeggio in every part of the neck, often in the same place, which is what lets a progression stay under one hand. The tap is the other half of the classic sound: one more note above the shape, played by the picking hand, so the arpeggio reaches higher than the fretting hand can stretch.
howTo: E-shape: the first note is on the A string, then one note a string up to the top, and a hammer to the top note. There's no second note on the A string, so the bottom turn is a pick turn, and the rest after each loop gives you time for it and a moment to check the mute.
Tap with the middle finger of the picking hand, holding the pick tucked against the palm. Tap firmly on the fret, then pull off slightly downward so the fretted note under it sounds.
While you tap, the fretting hand keeps holding the note you pull off to. The tap is a loud attack and it counts as a note that must be heard.
steps.payoff: Two five-string shapes per chord, and a tapped A minor sweep that reaches up to fret 20.

steps.title: Inversions and position shifts
steps.goal: Change five-string shape and position at the bar line with no gap and no lost notes.
steps.why: You now have shapes, and music asks for them in a hurry. A real progression doesn't wait while you find the next one, so this Step is where the shapes you own become usable: the hand travels in the time of one note, and the sweep picks up as if nothing happened.
howTo: Look at the next shape before you need it. The eye gets there first, then the hand.
Most of these moves happen in the last note of the bar. Let that note go, and be early rather than late.
Practise only the move first: the last two notes of the bar and the first two of the next.

steps.title: The link: two shapes
steps.goal: Get from one arpeggio into the next with no gap and no extra pick stroke, slowly enough to hear the join.
steps.why: Linked arpeggios are what make a sweep sound like a solo and not an exercise, and the link is a separate skill from either shape. Almost everyone practises the shapes and hopes the join comes along. It doesn't: the join is where the pick stops, the hand arrives late and a note gets lost. So here it gets practised alone, as slowly as you like, with nothing else to think about.
howTo: A link is one small move of the fretting hand. On the top or bottom string, step from the last note of the old shape to the nearest note of the new one with a hammer, a pull or a slide. The pick does nothing at that moment.
Choose the nearest note of the new chord, not the root. Good links barely move the hand, which is why the shapes here may look unfamiliar.
Look ahead. Know the note you are stepping to before you play the note you are stepping from.
Keep muting through the change: the last note of the old shape stops as the new one sounds.
steps.payoff: You hear one line carry on across a chord change, and a chord change that happens under your fingers instead of between two shapes.

steps.title: Chains of links
steps.goal: Link four chords in a row on three strings, without stopping, in any minor key.
steps.why: Once two shapes link, the question becomes how long you can keep it going. A four-chord chain is the unit of real playing, and the minor-key loops here are the most common things you will be asked to sweep over. The moves are small, so the hard part is keeping your place: you should know which chord is next without counting.
howTo: Learn the chords by ear first. Play the progression's roots, once through, on the low strings.
Each chord's shape starts as near as it can to the last one. Don't reach for the shape you know best: reach for the nearest one.
If a link trips you, go back to two shapes and repeat that one link. Don't push through it.
steps.payoff: A four-chord minor progression comes out of one unbroken sweep, in whichever key you land on today.

steps.title: Minor keys and the major five chord
steps.goal: Link through the harmonic-minor movement: the major five chord pulling back to the one chord.
steps.why: A natural-minor loop goes round forever and never needs to resolve. The major five chord is what changes that: its G# sits a half step under A and pulls back to it, and that pull is the dark, dramatic sound of metal and neoclassical playing. These progressions are shared vocabulary, and the thing to learn is the half-step move: it is the link you will come to love.
howTo: The chords of a key are numbered from its first note and written as Roman numerals, small for a minor chord and capital for a major one. In A minor the one chord is A minor (i), the four chord is D minor (iv), the five chord is E major (V) and the six chord is F major (VI). Chords in a Key teaches the numbers.
E major in A minor contains G#, a note A minor doesn't have. Find it in the shape. It is where the sound comes from.
Aim for the G# to A step at the resolution, and hear it before you play it.
Bdim to E to Am is the minor two-five-one. It is the same pull with one more chord of warning.
steps.payoff: You hear a chord pull back to the minor at the end of a sweep, and a progression sounds like it's going somewhere.

steps.title: Four and five strings, linked
steps.goal: Chain the big shapes, and mix short and long shapes in one line.
steps.why: The bigger the shape, the further the hand has to come back at the end of it, so links on five strings need more planning than links on three. It also pays best: this is the sound of a fast minor-key lead break. Mixing lengths matters too, because a line of one length sounds like a pattern, and a three-string shape in the middle of big ones gives you somewhere to breathe.
howTo: Plan the link from the bottom of each shape: the last note on the A string walks to the first note of the next shape.
With five strings there's a lot to keep silent, and the mute has to travel across every change as well.
Mixed lengths: keep the beat the same when the shape gets shorter. The short shape fills the bar with two loops.
steps.payoff: A long chain over a whole progression, big enough to sound like a solo.

steps.goal: Play four- and five-string sweeps that follow Am, F, C, G over a band, an eight-bar etude that uses the whole Level, and one chorus you put together yourself.
steps.why: Everything so far has been against a click. A band is different: the bass already plays the root, so your arpeggio can start somewhere else, and the drums will happily cover you if you get lost for a beat. This is where it stops being an exercise and sounds like what you hoped to play.
howTo: Keep the volume honest: if the band is covering your mistakes, turn it down until they show.
Use direct input or headphones for a graded take. A microphone also hears the band, and that hasn't been tested.
Start each version at a rung where you can look up from the guitar. You're playing with people now, even if the people are samples.
steps.payoff: You play a sweep arpeggio solo over a band, and it follows the chords.

exercises.title: With the band: four strings

howTo: Two loops a bar, at a tempo the band can really sit in. Up to about 100 BPM the app can help. Above that, record and listen.
exercises.coachLine: I can help on the slow rungs. Above them, a recording will tell you more than I can.

exercises.purpose: Eight bars written for this Path, using everything in the Level: A-shapes and E-shapes through Am, F, C and G, three-string loops through Dm and E, a tapped A minor, and a sweep up to a held high A.

steps.title: Six strings
steps.goal: Own a clean six-string sweep from the low E, minor and major, and link passes across all six.
steps.why: Six strings is the longest push you can make, and it is a real physical challenge, since the arm travels the whole width of the neck and every string behind the pick has to stay quiet. It adds less new music than the step from three to five did. Come to it for the sound and for the discipline: a clean six-string sweep shows up any weakness in your muting at once.
howTo: The arm does this. The wrist stays quiet, and the forearm carries the pick from the low E to the high E in one long push.
Muting is the whole game: palm on what's behind the pick, the fretting fingers rolling off what's in front of it. Low strings ring loudest, so check them first.
Grading on these is limited: only the slowest rungs are graded, and even those have never been tried on a real guitar.
steps.payoff: A sweep from the lowest note on the guitar to near the highest, with every note separate.

exercises.coachLine: Graded only to 100 BPM. Trust a recording above that: long sweeps are where I'm least sure of myself.

steps.title: Six strings through the changes
steps.goal: Change chord with the six-string shapes: a minor shape into its major, four chords in a minor key, and a six-string shape joined to a five-string and a three-string one.
steps.why: The last Step gave you two six-string shapes, each looped on one chord, and single passes linked through a progression. Looping a whole shape on each chord of a progression is harder: a shape this wide is slow to leave, with six strings to quiet and a new place to find before the next bar. This Step adds no new shape. It takes the minor and the major shape through changes, slowly, so the move between them gets the practice the shapes have already had.
howTo: Each bar is one chord. In the sixteenth-note lines every bar ends with a rest: stop every string in it, then move the hand.
The pass tempos are slow on purpose. These shapes are wide, and the change has to be clean before it is fast.
The minor shape: index and little finger on the low E, the ring finger rolling across the A and D strings, the index rolling across the G, B and top strings, and the little finger for the top hammer.

The major shape is fingered the same both ways: little finger on the low E, ring finger on the A string, the index rolling across the D and G strings, the middle finger on the B string, and the index again two frets lower on the top string.

Grading is timing only, as on the rest of the Path: how even the notes are, whether each one arrived, and whether extra notes rang. The fast rungs are not graded at all: there it is your ear and a recording.
steps.payoff: Six-string arpeggios that follow a chord progression, and a line where a big shape hands over to a small one without a stop.

exercises.title: Minor, then its relative major
exercises.purpose: The minor shape and the major shape from the last Step, one bar each, as one line. G major is the relative major of E minor: the major chord three frets above it. They share two of their three notes, G and B, so the two shapes sit around the same frets and only the change is new.

Bar 2 is G major: thirteen notes and three sixteenths of rest. It starts at fret 15 on the low E string, the note the E minor bar stopped on, and it comes back to that note.
In the G major bar the top string is played at fret 10 and hammered to fret 15. The index moves down two frets for it, and two frets back up for the G and D strings on the return.
Use each rest to stop all six strings before the next bar starts.
exercises.coachLine: Timing only: how even the notes are, whether each one arrived, and whether an extra one rang. The silence in the rests is yours to check.

exercises.purpose: A four-chord progression in C minor with a whole six-string shape on each chord: C minor, Ab, F minor and G. The last chord is the major five chord you met in the Step "Minor keys and the major five chord": the one that pulls the line back to the first.

C minor starts on the low E at fret 8. Ab starts on the low E at fret 16, with the little finger. That is the longest move in the line and the rest before it is the short one, so leave the first chord early rather than land late.

For G the little finger moves down one fret, to fret 15 on the low E. After that last bar the hand drops back to fret 8.

steps.title: Wide shapes and fast shifts
steps.goal: Jump between shapes far apart on the neck, and play sweeps fast enough that grading no longer applies.
steps.why: Most moves until now have been a fret or two. Sometimes a line needs an octave jump, and that's a throw of the whole arm that has to land exactly. This is also where speed comes in, so it's where the app can't help much: you'll be working by recording and by ear, as players always have.
howTo: Look at the landing spot before you leave. The hand follows the eye.
A shift is one fast movement and then stillness. Land early and let the note come to you.
Fast rungs are self-checked. Record yourself and slow the recording down: nothing is more honest than that.
steps.payoff: A line that jumps the neck, and a burst of sweep at a speed you couldn't have played a month ago.

steps.title: Neoclassical sequences
steps.goal: Play the moves that give this style its sound: diminished shapes climbing in minor thirds, and triads walking up the harmonic minor scale.
steps.why: Baroque-flavoured metal comes from a few harmonic ideas played very fast: the major five chord, the diminished seventh on its leading tone, and triads walked in sequence. You've met the first, and a diminished triad in the minor two-five-one. The diminished seventh adds one note to that triad, a half step under the home note. A sequence adds the sense of a long line unfolding, and a diminished chord that moves three frets at a time is the most fun you can have with one shape.
howTo: A diminished seventh is the same four notes every three frets. So G#dim7, Bdim7, Ddim7 and Fdim7 are one sound in four places.
In a sequence, hear each bar as the next step of one melody. The top notes usually tell the tale.
These are original lines in a shared style, and meant as starting points: write your own as soon as you can.
steps.payoff: The unmistakable sound of a neoclassical run, in lines you can change and call your own.

exercises.title: Diminished resolving to Am

howTo: G#dim7 at fret 10 and Bdim7 at fret 13 are the same four notes, played from different places. Only the shape's position changes.
Hear the G# pull up to A at the end of the line.
exercises.coachLine: Well done if this sounds dramatic. I report timing and notes heard; the sound is yours to judge.

steps.title: The Advanced etude
steps.goal: Play an eight-bar piece in E minor that puts the Level's moves together: six-string shapes, a diminished shape climbing the neck, a shift between positions and the major five chord pulling home, in two halves and then with a band.
steps.why: The Level has given you its moves one at a time: six strings, shifts, the diminished shape, the major five chord. A piece asks for them in a row with no time to set up, and that is a different skill from playing each one well. So it comes in halves: four bars until they hold, the next four, then the join, then the band.
howTo: The piece is eight bars of triplets in E minor: E minor, C, G and D# diminished 7, then E minor, A minor, B and E minor.
Parts one and two are against a click. Bring each to its pass tempo before joining them.
With the band, use direct input or headphones for a graded take: a microphone hears the band as well, and that has not been tested.

Grading is timing only: how even the notes are, whether each one arrived, and whether extra notes rang. Nothing here checks which notes you played or how clean the mute is, so record a take and listen.
steps.payoff: An eight-bar sweep solo over a band, with six-string shapes, a diminished climb and a major five chord in it, played from start to finish.

exercises.title: The etude, part one
exercises.purpose: The first four bars of the etude: E minor on six strings, C on five, G on six, then a diminished shape that climbs three frets and leaves the line waiting for an answer.
howTo: Triplets. Bar 1 is the six-string E minor shape from fret 12 with no hammer on the low E: twelve notes.
Bar 2 is C major on five strings, from fret 15 on the A string, one fret above the note bar 1 ended on. It ends with a two-note rest.
Bar 3 is the six-string G major shape, from the little finger at fret 15 on the low E, up to the top-string hammer and back to the A string: twelve notes, no rest.

Bar 4 is D# diminished 7 on three strings: one loop from fret 14 on the G string, then the same shape three frets higher, from fret 17. Little finger on the G string, ring on the B string, index on the top string, and the little finger again for the hammer. The pick skips the D string to get there from bar 3, and the index drops from fret 12 to fret 11.
When it loops, the diminished bar pulls back to the E minor of bar 1. That jump back to the low E is not in the piece, so do not let it hold you at a rung.
exercises.coachLine: Big shapes and small ones in one line. The notes are timed and counted; whether the changes sound like one line is for you and a recording.

exercises.title: The etude, part two
exercises.purpose: The last four bars of the etude, bars 5 to 8, as the answer: E minor high on the neck, A minor below it, B major pulling home, and one sweep up all six strings to a held E.
howTo: Triplets. Bar 1 here, bar 5 of the piece, is E minor on three strings, two loops: fret 16 on the G string, 17 on the B string, 15 on the top string, and a hammer to fret 19.
Bar 2 is A minor, two loops: fret 14 on the G string, 13 on the B string, 12 on the top string, and a hammer to fret 17. The index moves down three frets to get there.

Bar 3 is B major: one loop from fret 11 on the G string, then the upstroke carries on through the G string again, the D string at fret 13 and the A string at fret 14. A beat of rest follows. B major has a D# in it, at fret 11 on the top string, one fret below the E that the last bar holds: that half step is the pull home.
Bar 4 is the six-string E minor shape with its hammer on the low E, swept once from fret 12 to the top string. The E there, at fret 12, is held for two beats with vibrato.
exercises.coachLine: The beat of silence in bar 3 here (bar 7 of the piece) is part of the music: stop the strings in it. Timing and notes heard are reported, and the held E is yours to judge.

steps.title: A heavy band, a long line
steps.goal: Play linked five- and six-string sweeps over a band in a minor key, and make your own chorus from them.
steps.why: It's the point of the whole Level. A loud band sits on the low strings and leaves the top of the neck to you, so a long sweep cuts through. It also hides your mistakes, which is why a recording matters even more here than before.
howTo: Turn the band down until your mistakes show.
Use direct input or headphones for any graded take: a microphone hears the band as well, and that hasn't been tested.
Grading covers the slower rungs only. Above them you're on your own, with your ears and a recording.
